issues.title: [inductor] baddbmm with broadcast bias: autotune never considers the bmm + pointwise-bias decomposition (1.3-1.45x left on the table at MoE expert-GEMM shapes)
issues.author: cfregly
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug For `baddbmm` with a **broadcast** bias (`bias[B, 1, N]`, stride `[N, 0, 1]` after broadcasting), Inductor's max-autotune chooses between (a) Triton templates and (b) the extern ATen kernel — but never considers the decomposition `bmm(x, w) + bias`, which is faster than both of its existing choices whenever the bias add can fuse into a neighboring pointwise op (which in MLP/MoE blocks it essentially always can — there is an activation right after the GEMM). Why both existing choices lose at this shape (`[32, 640, 1024] x [32, 1024, 2048] + bias[32, 1, 2048]`, bf16, sm_103): * **Extern `baddbmm` is honestly slow** (this is *not* an autotune measurement bug — we verified the benchmarked number is the true per-call cost): cuBLAS computes `C = alpha*A@B + beta*C`, so `at::baddbmm_out` must first materialize the broadcast bias into the output buffer. With a stride-0 bias dim that is a full `[B, M, N]`-sized strided elementwise copy (~75 us here), followed by a beta=1 GEMM that re-reads those bytes (~67 us): ~138 us per call, every call. * **The Triton template wins the autotune for the op as written** (~104-106 us; it reads the `[B, 1, N]` bias in its epilogue for free), so this is what Inductor ships. * **The missing candidate is faster than both:** `bmm` routes extern to a beta=0 kernel (~60-62 us — C is never read or pre-filled), and the rank-1 bias add fuses into the adjacent pointwise. Measured with the GELU consumer present (the realistic MLP/MoE shape of the graph): `gelu(baddbmm(...))` = 168.1 us/call vs `gelu(bmm(...) + bias)` = 115.8 us/call — **1.45x** for the GEMM+activation pair. In the full MoE layer this came out to **1.31x end-to-end** (0.407 ms -> 0.311 ms median, verified numerics). Kernel-level view (torch profiler, per call, GB300): | graph as written | decomposed | |---|---| | `triton_tem_fused_baddbmm_0` 105.9 us | `nvjet_..._bz_NNT` (extern beta=0 bmm) 61.7 us | | `triton_poi_fused_gelu_1` 69.3 us | `triton_poi_fused_add_gelu_0` 56.0 us | Standalone (no consumer to fuse the bias add into), the decomposition is *not* a win (102.2 vs 104.7 us here) — which is exactly why this wants to be an autotune-level choice (benchmarked in graph context, where the scheduler knows whether the epilogue can fuse) or a decomposition with a consumer-aware condition, rather than an unconditional rewrite. Possibly related: the ATen-level cost itself (broadcast-bias `baddbmm` paying a full output-sized materialization copy: 138.0 us vs 60.3 us for the bare `bmm`, eager) could separately be improved in cuBLAS dispatch (e.g. via a fused-epilogue path), but the Inductor decomposition choice is the more general fix and is what this issue asks for. ### Repro Standalone script attached (`repro.py`, no external deps). It compiles both formulations with `mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs"`, prints per-call timings + the kernels each compiled graph runs, and asserts the template choice and the gap. Output on a GB300 (sm_103): ``` eager baddbmm (broadcast bias [B,1,N]): 138.0 us/call eager bmm (no bias) : 60.3 us/call compiled baddbmm (bare) : 102.2 us/call compiled bmm + bias (bare) : 104.7 us/call compiled gelu(baddbmm) (as written) : 168.1 us/call compiled gelu(bmm+bias) (decomposed) : 115.8 us/call decomposition speedup with consumer : 1.451x ``` ### Suggested fix Register a decomposition (or an additional autotune candidate) for `baddbmm` when the bias input has a stride-0 broadcast dim: `bmm(batch1, batch2) + input`. The pointwise add participates in normal Inductor fusion, so wherever the GEMM output feeds a pointwise op the bias is free; the autotuner's existing benchmarking would keep the current behavior in the (rarer) standalone case if the candidate loses there. ### Versions * torch 2.12.0a0 (NGC 26.05 container build), CUDA 13.2, driver 580.159.03 * GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (sm_103); shapes are MoE expert-GEMM class (`E=32` experts, `tokens*capacity=640`, `hidden=1024`, `ffn=2048`, bf16) * Reproduces with caches disabled (`TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES=1`)
repro.py (standalone, no external deps) ```python # Standalone reproducer: torch.compile (Inductor, max-autotune GEMM tuning) # never considers the `bmm + pointwise bias` decomposition as an autotune # choice for `baddbmm` with a BROADCAST bias, leaving measurable performance # on the table at MoE expert-GEMM shapes. # # Mechanism (all autotune numbers honest, none of this is a benchmark bug): # * For `baddbmm(bias[B,1,N], x[B,M,K], w[B,K,N])` the extern (cuBLAS/ATen) # choice is honestly slow: cuBLAS computes C = alpha*A@B + beta*C, so # `at::baddbmm_out` must first MATERIALIZE the broadcast bias into the # output buffer (a strided elementwise copy over the full [B,M,N] output) # and then run a beta=1 GEMM that re-reads it. # * The Triton template, which reads the [B,1,N] bias in its epilogue for # free, therefore wins the autotune FOR THE OP AS WRITTEN. # * But the decomposition `bmm(x, w) + bias` is faster than BOTH: the pure # GEMM routes extern to a beta=0 kernel (C never read), and the rank-1 # bias add is a cheap pointwise kernel that Inductor can fuse into # neighboring ops in real graphs (where it becomes effectively free). # # This script compiles both forms at a representative shape, both bare and # with the activation that follows the GEMM in any MLP/MoE block (GELU), # prints the kernels each compiled graph actually runs, and asserts: # 1. compiled baddbmm keeps a Triton GEMM template; the decomposed form # routes the GEMM to an extern beta=0 kernel (no Triton template), # 2. with the activation consumer present (the realistic case), the # decomposed form is faster end-to-end: the bias add fuses into the # activation pointwise for free, # 3. eager baddbmm with a broadcast bias is much slower than eager bmm # (the ATen materialization cost itself). # # The bare (no-consumer) pair is also timed and printed: standalone, the # unfused bias add costs more than the template's free epilogue read, which # is exactly why this should be an AUTOTUNE-LEVEL DECOMPOSITION CHOICE # (benchmarked in graph context, where pointwise fusion applies) rather # than an unconditional decomposition. # # Tested environment: NVIDIA GB300 (sm_103), CUDA 13.2, driver 580.159.03, # torch 2.12.0a0 (NGC 26.05). No repo dependencies. import os # Fresh tune every run: keep the experiment hermetic. os.environ.setdefault("TORCHINDUCTOR_FORCE_DISABLE_CACHES", "1") import torch # noqa: E402 B, M, K, N = 32, 640, 1024, 2048 # MoE expert GEMM1 class (bf16) DTYPE = torch.bfloat16 WARMUP, ITERS = 20, 200 def cuda_time_us(fn, *args): for _ in range(WARMUP): fn(*args) torch.cuda.synchronize() beg = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) beg.record() for _ in range(ITERS): fn(*args) end.record() torch.cuda.synchronize() return beg.elapsed_time(end) * 1000.0 / ITERS def gpu_kernels(fn, *args): """Names + total us of CUDA kernels per call (5-call profile).""" from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile fn(*args) # ensure compiled torch.cuda.synchronize() with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof: for _ in range(5): fn(*args) torch.cuda.synchronize() out = {} for evt in prof.key_averages(): if evt.device_type == torch.autograd.DeviceType.CUDA and evt.self_device_time_total > 0: out[evt.key] = out.get(evt.key, 0.0) + evt.self_device_time_total / 5.0 return out def op_baddbmm(bias, x, w): return torch.baddbmm(bias, x, w) def op_bmm_bias(bias, x, w): return torch.bmm(x, w) + bias def op_baddbmm_gelu(bias, x, w): return torch.nn.functional.gelu(torch.baddbmm(bias, x, w)) def op_bmm_bias_gelu(bias, x, w): return torch.nn.functional.gelu(torch.bmm(x, w) + bias) def main(): assert torch.cuda.is_available() torch.manual_seed(42) dev = "cuda" x = torch.randn(B, M, K, device=dev, dtype=DTYPE) w = torch.randn(B, K, N, device=dev, dtype=DTYPE) bias = torch.randn(B, 1, N, device=dev, dtype=DTYPE) # broadcast over M # --- eager: the ATen-level cost of the broadcast-bias materialization --- t_eager_baddbmm = cuda_time_us(op_baddbmm, bias, x, w) t_eager_bmm = cuda_time_us(torch.bmm, x, w) print(f"eager baddbmm (broadcast bias [B,1,N]): {t_eager_baddbmm:8.1f} us/call") print(f"eager bmm (no bias) : {t_eager_bmm:8.1f} us/call") # --- compiled: what Inductor picks for each formulation --- compiled_baddbmm = torch.compile( op_baddbmm, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs" ) compiled_bmm_bias = torch.compile( op_bmm_bias, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs" ) t_c_baddbmm = cuda_time_us(compiled_baddbmm, bias, x, w) t_c_bmm_bias = cuda_time_us(compiled_bmm_bias, bias, x, w) print(f"compiled baddbmm (bare) : {t_c_baddbmm:8.1f} us/call") print(f"compiled bmm + bias (bare) : {t_c_bmm_bias:8.1f} us/call") print(" (bare, the unfused bias add costs more than the template's free" " epilogue read — the decomposition only pays in graph context)") # --- compiled, with the activation consumer (the realistic MLP/MoE case) compiled_baddbmm_gelu = torch.compile( op_baddbmm_gelu, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs", ) compiled_decomposed_gelu = torch.compile( op_bmm_bias_gelu, fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs", ) t_c_baddbmm_gelu = cuda_time_us(compiled_baddbmm_gelu, bias, x, w) t_c_decomposed_gelu = cuda_time_us(compiled_decomposed_gelu, bias, x, w) print(f"compiled gelu(baddbmm) (as written) : {t_c_baddbmm_gelu:8.1f} us/call") print(f"compiled gelu(bmm+bias) (decomposed) : {t_c_decomposed_gelu:8.1f} us/call") print(f"decomposition speedup with consumer : " f"{t_c_baddbmm_gelu / t_c_decomposed_gelu:8.3f}x") # numerics: identical inputs, compare outputs ref = op_baddbmm_gelu(bias.float(), x.float(), w.float()) out_a = compiled_baddbmm_gelu(bias, x, w).float() out_b = compiled_decomposed_gelu(bias, x, w).float() for name, out in (("gelu(baddbmm)", out_a), ("gelu(bmm+bias)", out_b)): rel = (out - ref).abs().max() / ref.abs().max() print(f"max rel err vs fp32 ref, {name:15s}: {rel.item():.3e}") assert rel < 2e-2, f"{name} numerics off" kerns_a = gpu_kernels(compiled_baddbmm_gelu, bias, x, w) kerns_b = gpu_kernels(compiled_decomposed_gelu, bias, x, w) print("\nkernels, compiled gelu(baddbmm):") for k, v in sorted(kerns_a.items(), key=lambda i: -i[1]): print(f" {v:9.1f} us {k}") print("kernels, compiled gelu(bmm + bias):") for k, v in sorted(kerns_b.items(), key=lambda i: -i[1]): print(f" {v:9.1f} us {k}") # 1. template choice: baddbmm keeps a Triton template GEMM; the # decomposition routes the GEMM extern (cuBLAS), no template survives. a_has_template = any("triton_tem" in k for k in kerns_a) b_has_template = any("triton_tem" in k for k in kerns_b) assert a_has_template, ( "expected compiled gelu(baddbmm) to pick a Triton GEMM template " f"(got: {sorted(kerns_a)})" ) assert not b_has_template, ( "expected compiled gelu(bmm+bias) to route the GEMM extern " f"(got: {sorted(kerns_b)})" ) # 2. with the consumer present, the decomposition is faster end-to-end. assert t_c_baddbmm_gelu / t_c_decomposed_gelu > 1.05, ( f"decomposition not faster with consumer: " f"{t_c_baddbmm_gelu:.1f} vs {t_c_decomposed_gelu:.1f} us" ) # 3. ATen-level: broadcast-bias baddbmm pays a full output-sized # materialization copy before the GEMM. assert t_eager_baddbmm / t_eager_bmm > 1.5, ( f"expected eager broadcast-bias baddbmm >> eager bmm: " f"{t_eager_baddbmm:.1f} vs {t_eager_bmm:.1f} us" ) print("\nALL ASSERTIONS PASSED — Inductor lacks the bmm+pointwise-bias " "decomposition choice for broadcast-bias baddbmm.") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```

issues.title: torch.compile recompiles when input alternates between AsyncCollectiveTensor and Tensor
issues.author: HosseinKaviani-H
issues.body:
### torch.compile recompiles when input alternates between AsyncCollectiveTensor and Tensor

## Summary

When a compiled region's input alternates between `AsyncCollectiveTensor` (ACT)
and a resolved `Tensor` across steps, Dynamo guards on the tensor class and
recompiles each time the class changes. With FSDP + TP this happens during the
first several steps (all-gathered weights are natively `AsyncCollectiveTensor`,
but get resolved to a plain `Tensor` once awaited before the compiled region by
prefetch/overlap scheduling), forcing users to raise
`torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit` well above the default of 8.

The all-gather output is fundamentally an `AsyncCollectiveTensor`; the plain
`Tensor` case only arises when the ACT is awaited before the compiled region.
So the direction that matters here is **trace with ACT, then provide a resolved
`Tensor` at runtime** — which the runtime wrapper already handles by unwrapping
ACT. Relaxing the class guard for *this* direction should be safe, and would
avoid the wasted recompiles.

(Note the reverse direction — trace with `Tensor`, then provide an un-awaited
ACT at runtime — is *not* safe to relax, since the traced graph may skip the
await; this repro deliberately does not exercise that direction.)

## Repro

```python
# TORCH_LOGS=recompiles torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 repro.py
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
from torch.distributed._functional_collectives import all_gather_tensor

dist.init_process_group("nccl")
rank = dist.get_rank()
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
device = torch.device(f"cuda:{rank}")

@torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
def step(x, w):
    return (x @ w).sum()

x = torch.randn(8, 8, device=device)
w_shard = torch.randn(4, 8, device=device)   # each rank holds 4 rows

# Step 0 traces with ACT (the native all-gather output); step 1 provides a
# resolved Tensor. This is the safe-to-relax direction (ACT at trace -> Tensor
# at runtime), which the runtime wrapper already handles by unwrapping ACT.
for i in range(6):
    w = all_gather_tensor(w_shard, gather_dim=0, group=dist.group.WORLD)
    if i % 2 == 1:
        # resolve to a plain Tensor before the compiled region
        w = torch.ops._c10d_functional.wait_tensor(w)
    # else (incl. step 0): pass the AsyncCollectiveTensor straight in
    out = step(x, w)
    if rank == 0:
        print(f"step {i}: type(w)={type(w).__name__}, out={out.item():.4f}")

dist.destroy_process_group()
```

Run with:
```
TORCH_LOGS=recompiles torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 repro.py
```

## Expected

The compiled region treats `AsyncCollectiveTensor` (which is awaited before
execution) and the resolved `Tensor` as equivalent — one compiled graph, no
recompiles after the first.

## Actual

Dynamo emits a recompile each time the tensor class changes. Captured output
(`TORCH_LOGS=recompiles`), here at step 1 when the resolved `Tensor` arrives
after step 0 traced with ACT:
```
TORCH_LOGS=recompiles torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 scripts/repro_async_collective_recompile.py
W0611 15:02:26.326000 2128124 site-packages/torch/distributed/run.py:852] 
W0611 15:02:26.326000 2128124 site-packages/torch/distributed/run.py:852] *****************************************
W0611 15:02:26.326000 2128124 site-packages/torch/distributed/run.py:852] Setting OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable for each process to be 1 in default, to avoid your system being overloaded, please further tune the variable for optimal performance in your application as needed. 
W0611 15:02:26.326000 2128124 site-packages/torch/distributed/run.py:852] *****************************************
NCCL version 2.27.5+cuda12.9
step 0: type(w)=AsyncCollectiveTensor, out=9.8565
[rank0]:V0611 15:02:33.918000 2129572 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles] Recompiling function step in /home/hosseinkh/pytorch/torchtitan_local/scripts/repro_async_collective_recompile.py:32
[rank0]:V0611 15:02:33.918000 2129572 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles]     triggered by the following guard failure(s):
[rank0]:V0611 15:02:33.918000 2129572 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles]     - 0/0: ___check_type_id(w, 114219360), type=<class 'torch.distributed._functional_collectives.AsyncCollectiveTensor'>  # return (x @ w).sum()  # pytorch/torchtitan_local/scripts/repro_async_collective_recompile.py:34 in step
[rank1]:V0611 15:02:33.964000 2129573 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles] Recompiling function step in /home/hosseinkh/pytorch/torchtitan_local/scripts/repro_async_collective_recompile.py:32
[rank1]:V0611 15:02:33.964000 2129573 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles]     triggered by the following guard failure(s):
[rank1]:V0611 15:02:33.964000 2129573 site-packages/torch/_dynamo/guards.py:4514] [0/1] [__recompiles]     - 0/0: ___check_type_id(w, 114221808), type=<class 'torch.distributed._functional_collectives.AsyncCollectiveTensor'>  # return (x @ w).sum()  # pytorch/torchtitan_local/scripts/repro_async_collective_recompile.py:34 in step
step 1: type(w)=Tensor, out=9.8565
step 2: type(w)=AsyncCollectiveTensor, out=9.8565
step 3: type(w)=Tensor, out=9.8565
step 4: type(w)=AsyncCollectiveTensor, out=9.8565
step 5: type(w)=Tensor, out=9.8565

Note: `out` is identical every step — the two compiled graphs are equivalent, so the recompile from the tensor-class guard is wasted.
```

Note the output is identical every step (the exact value varies per run since
`w` is randomly initialized, but it is constant *within* a run), confirming the
two compiled graphs are equivalent — the recompile is wasted.

## Impact

In TorchTitan's HuggingFace SFT backend (FSDP + TP + compile), this is one of
several guard sources that pushed recompiles past the default
`cache_size_limit=8`, causing `FailOnRecompileLimitHit` with `fullgraph=True`.
Workaround was raising the limit to 64. The recompiles stabilize after ~3-5
steps once the tensor classes settle.

## Environment

- PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu128
- CUDA: 12.8
- GPU: NVIDIA H100 (×8)

## Workaround

```python
torch._dynamo.config.cache_size_limit = 64
```

## Question

Can the class-level guard treat a runtime `Tensor` as compatible with a graph
traced on `AsyncCollectiveTensor` (the ACT-at-trace -> Tensor-at-runtime
direction)? The runtime wrapper already unwraps ACT, so the resolved tensors
produce an equivalent graph, and this is the direction FSDP + TP actually hits.

The reverse direction (Tensor-at-trace -> ACT-at-runtime) should *not* be
relaxed: per discussion, there are cases where the runtime wrapper does not
await ACT until pytorch/pytorch#186442 lands, so relaxing that direction could
silently use an un-awaited ACT.



### Versions

PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu128
CUDA: 12.8
GPU: NVIDIA H100 (×8)

issues.title: nn.Module.to() fails on a tensor-subclass parameter held by an EMA / external weakref (forced swap_tensors path, no compile)
issues.author: ultism
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`nn.Module._apply` unconditionally takes the `torch.utils.swap_tensors()` path for **traceable-wrapper-subclass** parameters (because `set_data` cannot rebind a subclass). `swap_tensors()` refuses any tensor that has a weakref associated with it. As a result, **if anything holds a `weakref` to a tensor-subclass parameter, the module can never be moved again with `.to()` / `.cpu()` / `.cuda()` / a dtype cast** — it raises `_apply(): Couldn't swap <Module>.weight`.

A very common trigger is **EMA**: `torch_ema`, `timm`'s `ModelEmaV2`, and most hand-rolled EMA implementations keep a `weakref.ref` to every tracked parameter (so the EMA does not keep the model alive). EMA over a model that has tensor-subclass parameters — e.g. a [torchao](https://github.com/pytorch/ao) fp8 / quantized weight subclass — therefore makes the model un-`.to()`-able for the rest of training (offload, device move, dtype cast all fail).

This needs **no `torch.compile` and no `FakeTensorMode`**, and the `swap_module_params_on_conversion` future flag is **off** — the swap path is forced purely by the parameter being a subclass.

#### Repro (self-contained, CPU, no compile)

```python
import torch
import weakref
from torch.testing._internal.two_tensor import TwoTensor
from torch.utils._python_dispatch import is_traceable_wrapper_subclass


class EMA:
    """Minimal EMA, exactly how torch_ema / common impls track params: a weakref per
    parameter (so the EMA does not keep the model alive)."""
    def __init__(self, params):
        params = list(params)
        self.shadow = [p.detach().clone() for p in params]
        self._refs = [weakref.ref(p) for p in params]   # <-- the persistent weakref


def make_model():
    a = torch.randn(8, 8)
    w = TwoTensor(a, a.clone())                     # any traceable wrapper subclass param
    assert is_traceable_wrapper_subclass(w)
    m = torch.nn.Linear(8, 8, bias=False)
    m.weight = torch.nn.Parameter(w, requires_grad=False)
    return m


print("swap_module_params_on_conversion:",
      torch.__future__.get_swap_module_params_on_conversion(), "(off -> swap forced by subclass-ness)")

m = make_model()
m.to(torch.float64)
print("[no EMA]      m.to(float64): OK")

m = make_model()
ema = EMA([m.weight])
try:
    m.to(torch.float64)
    print("[EMA alive]   m.to(float64): OK (no crash)")
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("[EMA alive]   m.to(float64): CRASH:", str(e).splitlines()[-1])

del ema
import gc; gc.collect()
m.to(torch.float64)
print("[EMA dropped] m.to(float64): OK")
```

#### Output

```
swap_module_params_on_conversion: False (off -> swap forced by subclass-ness)
[no EMA]      m.to(float64): OK
[EMA alive]   m.to(float64): CRASH: _apply(): Couldn't swap Linear.weight
[EMA dropped] m.to(float64): OK
```

The underlying error is `RuntimeError: Cannot swap t1 because it has weakref associated with it`, raised from `torch/utils/__init__.py` inside `nn.Module._apply` → `torch.utils.swap_tensors(param, param_applied)`.

#### Why this looks distinct from existing reports

Same underlying `_apply`-forces-swap / `swap_tensors`-rejects-weakref limitation as a few other issues, but the **weakref source — and therefore the fix — is different**:

- **#170770 / #141548** — weakref comes from `FakeTensorMode` / `MetaConverter` after `torch.compile`. The fix discussed there (clear the FakeTensorMode memos at end of compile, e.g. #171209) does **not** help this case: the EMA weakref lives in the EMA object, not in any fake-tensor cache.
- **#186796** — weakref comes from Dynamo guards on a *live compiled* module.
- **#145529** — requires `set_swap_module_params_on_conversion(True)` and is inside `@torch.compile`. Here the flag is off and there is no compile.
- **#170137** — same spirit (a tool's weakref blocks swap) but for the memory profiler on regular tensors.

So an EMA (or any user-held weakref) over a subclass-parameter model is an independent, compile-free manifestation that none of the above fixes would address. Because subclass params take the swap path *unconditionally*, there is also no `swap_module_params_on_conversion=False` escape hatch.

#### Possible directions (deferring to maintainers)

Either the subclass swap path in `_apply` could tolerate pre-existing weakrefs, or there could be a supported way to move a subclass-parameter module that has external (e.g. EMA) weakrefs.

### Versions

torch 2.12.0+cu130. The mechanism (`_apply` forcing `swap_tensors` for subclass params + `swap_tensors` rejecting weakrefs) is long-standing and version-independent, so this should reproduce on `main` / nightly as well.

### Technical Summary of the Fix:
- **Root Cause:** The `RuntimeError` originates from the Python-level checks (`weakref.getweakrefs`) inside `torch.utils.swap_tensors` which unconditionally reject tensors with active Python-level weak references.

comments.author: sebsv123
comments.body:
The crash root cause is a combination of two things hitting Inductor's lowering path simultaneously:

**1. `b.flatten()` as the bias argument to `conv2d`**

`F.conv2d` expects bias as a 1D tensor of shape `[out_channels]`. Here `b` has shape `[1, 1, 1, 1]` (same as input), so `b.flatten()` produces a 1-element 1D tensor — which is valid for eager. However, Inductor's lowering for `aten.convolution` needs to trace the bias through its own `View` lowering first, and the `flatten()` introduces a `view` node in the FX graph that Inductor's conv lowering doesn't handle when it appears inline as a bias operand. The `NotImplementedError: View` is thrown because Inductor tries to lower `view` as a standalone op inside the convolution lowering context where it's not expected.

**2. The `bool → float` cast chain**

`x.to(torch.bool).float()` produces a tensor where values are exactly `0.0` or `1.0`, which is fine numerically. But the cast chain creates two type-conversion nodes (`to(bool)` then `to(float)`) that Inductor may not fold into a single cast before reaching the conv lowering, potentially causing the view-resolution to fail on a tensor whose provenance it doesn't fully track.

**Minimal repro that isolates the `flatten()` issue:**
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# This crashes:
b = torch.ones(1, 1, 1, 1)
torch.compile(lambda x: F.conv2d(x, x, x.flatten()))(b)

# This does NOT crash (explicit reshape instead of flatten):
torch.compile(lambda x: F.conv2d(x, x, x.reshape(-1)))(b)
```
If `reshape` doesn't crash but `flatten` does, that confirms the issue is specifically in how Inductor lowers `aten.flatten` (which decomposes to `aten.view`) when it appears as a bias source in the conv lowering path.

**Workaround until fixed:**
```python
class M(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        b = x.to(torch.bool).float()
        bias = b.reshape(-1)  # use reshape instead of flatten
        return F.conv2d(b, b, bias, stride=1, padding=0)
```

The fix likely lives in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` in the `convolution` lowering handler — it needs to materialize/realize the bias tensor before entering the conv lowering, similar to how weight is handled.

issues.title: `torch.compile(dynamic=True)` backward fails with `InductorError: CantSplit` on chained residual blocks scattering into a wider buffer
issues.author: TheoBoyer
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug


A small model with two chained `x + Linear(RMSNorm(x))` residual blocks, where the residual buffer is built by scattering into a wider zero tensor, should compile and train fine under `torch.compile(..., dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)`.

**Expected:** compiled forward + backward run the same as eager.

**Actual:** eager works. The compiled forward also works. Only the **backward** fails, with `InductorError: CantSplit` raised from `_split_iteration_ranges`. The failing divisibility check is of the form `128 · X · (N + 1)` over `X · (N + 1)` — the quotient is the constant `128`, but Inductor reports it as not divisible.

### Minimal repro on a colab with t4 runtime

```python
"""
Previous cell: !pip install --upgrade torch torchvision torchaudio
"""

import os
os.environ["TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE"] = "1"
import torch

print("Torch version:", torch.__version__) # Torch version: 2.12.0+cu130

class M(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.n1 = torch.nn.RMSNorm(d)
        self.l1 = torch.nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)
        self.n2 = torch.nn.RMSNorm(d)
        self.l2 = torch.nn.Linear(d, d, bias=False)

    def forward(self, a, b):
        m = a.shape[0] // b.shape[0]
        out = torch.zeros(m * (b.shape[0] + 1), a.shape[-1], device=a.device)
        out[: a.shape[0]] = a
        out = out + self.l1(self.n1(out))
        out = out + self.l2(self.n2(out))
        return out.sum()

dev = "cuda"
a, b = torch.randn(21, 128, device=dev), torch.randn(7, device=dev)
print("Testing eager mode...")
M().to(dev)(a, b).backward()
print("Eager mode OK")
print("Testing compiled mode...")
torch.compile(M().to(dev), fullgraph=True, dynamic=True)(a, b).backward() # Crashes
print("Compiled mode OK")
```


### Trigger conditions (empirically minimized)

Tried each of the following in isolation that made the bug disappears:

1. **Scatter (`index_put`) into a wider buffer** using shape-derived indices (`out[: a.shape[0]] = a`). Replacing with `torch.cat` makes the bug vanish.
2. **`torch.compile(..., dynamic=True)`** with two free shape symbols (`T*N` and `N`), so `T = TN // N` becomes a `FloorDiv` in the symbolic env.
3. **At least two `x + Linear(RMSNorm(x))` residual blocks chained.** One block, zero `Linear`s, or zero `RMSNorm`s compiles fine.

comments.body:
Ran into this too while experimenting with dynamic shapes on residual architectures. A few observations that might help narrow it down:

The CantSplit error trace points to `_split_iteration_ranges` in `simd.py` failing on the expression `128*s52*((s97//s52)) + 128*((s97//s52))` not being divisible by `s52*((s97//s52)) + ((s97//s52))`. The quotient is trivially `128` (a compile-time constant), but the symbolic engine doesn't simplify `(s52 + 1) * k` over `(s52 + 1) * k` before checking divisibility, so it bails.

This seems related to how `FloorDiv` symbols compose when you have two free shape dimensions (`T*N` and `N`) — the `T = TN // N` substitution produces a `FloorDiv` node that doesn't get cancelled in the divisibility check even when the result is constant.

A workaround that avoids the crash: replace the scatter pattern with `torch.cat`:
```python
# Instead of:
out = torch.zeros(m * (b.shape[0] + 1), a.shape[-1], device=a.device)
out[: a.shape[0]] = a

# Use:
padding = torch.zeros(m * (b.shape[0] + 1) - a.shape[0], a.shape[-1], device=a.device)
out = torch.cat([a, padding], dim=0)
```
This compiles and runs the backward fine under `dynamic=True`. Confirmed it also regresses between 2.11 and 2.12 as TheoBoyer noted.

issues.title: [Inductor] ConvTranspose2d crashes with NoValidChoicesError when max_autotune_conv_backends=TRITON
issues.author: XAheli
issues.body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with `max_autotune_conv_backends = "TRITON"` crashes with `NoValidChoicesError` for transposed convolutions (`ConvTranspose2d`), dilated convolutions, and any convolution configuration that the forward Triton template doesn't support.

The original issue #125728 was closed in because regular `Conv2d` with TRITON backend was fixed. But transposed convolutions (and dilated convolutions) hit a different code path — the forward `convolution()` lowering in `torch/_inductor/kernel/conv.py` has no ATEN fallback safety net when the Triton template guard rejects the configuration, unlike the backward path added in #178945.

Related: #151555 (feature request for full Triton conv support)

### Repro

```python
import torch
import torch._inductor.config

torch._inductor.config.max_autotune = True
torch._inductor.config.max_autotune_conv_backends = "TRITON"

class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv_transpose2d = torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 128, kernel_size=(3, 5))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.conv_transpose2d(x)

m = Model().cuda()
m_compiled = torch.compile(m)
x = torch.randn(64, 64, 128, 256, device="cuda")
out = m_compiled(x)  # NoValidChoicesError
```

### Error

```
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: LoweringException: NoValidChoicesError: No choices to select.
Provided reason: No choices exist for backend. please consider adding ATEN into
max_autotune_conv_backends config (defined in torch/_inductor/config.py) to allow at least one choice.
  target: aten.convolution.default
  args[6]: True   # transposed=True
```
### Root Cause

The Triton template guard at `conv.py:616-625` rejects transposed convolutions (`and not transposed`), non-unit dilation (`and is_ones(dilation)`), and non-zero output_padding (`and is_zeros(output_padding)`). When `max_autotune_conv_backends = "TRITON"` (no ATEN), the `choices` list stays empty and `autotune_select_algorithm` raises `NoValidChoicesError`.

The backward path (PR #178945) handles this correctly with a two-tier fallback. The forward path has no equivalent safety net.


### Affected configurations 

| Configuration | Example |
|---|---|
| ConvTranspose1d | `nn.ConvTranspose1d(16, 32, 3)` |
| ConvTranspose2d | `nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 32, 3)` |
| ConvTranspose3d | `nn.ConvTranspose3d(16, 32, 3)` |
| Conv2d dilation>1 | `nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, dilation=2)` |
| ConvTranspose2d with output_padding | `nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 32, 3, stride=2, output_padding=1)` |


Versions
```
PyTorch: 2.13.0a0 (main @ ec2def0)
Triton: 3.7.0
GPU: NVIDIA H200
CUDA: 12.8

```

issues.title: [Inductor][AOTI] codegen_symbol uses float reciprocal for integer dim recovery, silently corrupts dynamic batches when 1/K is not exactly representable in IEEE-754
issues.author: pjh4993
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package` produces a package whose compiled forward silently returns wrong output rows whenever it has to recover a symbolic batch dim `s` from an input shape `K*s` and `(1.0/K)*K != 1.0` in IEEE-754 double precision. For non-power-of-2 `K` (e.g. `K=1496`, common in vision-tower token-grid shapes), the corruption hits at multiple runtime batch sizes — including the most degenerate case `bs=1`, which crashes inside `flash_attention` because the recovered batch evaluates to `0`.

Eager forward of the same `nn.Module` is correct at every batch on every version tested.

The bug is a composition of two PRs that are each individually correct:
- **#95698** (Mar 2023): made `CppPrinter._print_Rational` emit float division, intentionally, to fix `upsample_bilinear2d` / `upsample_nearest` dynamic-shape regressions (those ops need real fractional scale factors).
- **#146044** (Jan 2025): added composed-constraint dim recovery in `cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:codegen_symbol`, lowering `try_solve` results through the same `CppPrinter`. This routes integer dim recovery through the float-div printer.

Issue #145500 (the motivating bug for #146044) only used `K=2`, which is exactly representable, so the bug never surfaced in regression tests.


### Minimal reproducer (~30 lines, no extra deps)

```python
import os
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.export import Dim

D    = int(os.environ.get("D", 1280))
H    = int(os.environ.get("H", 16))
HD   = int(os.environ.get("HD", 80))
L    = int(os.environ.get("L", 1496))    # any K such that (1.0/K)*K != 1.0 reproduces
MAXN = int(os.environ.get("MAXN", 8))
assert D == H * HD


class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(D, 3 * D)
        self.out = nn.Linear(D, D)
    def forward(self, x, sizes):
        torch._check(x.shape[0] == sizes.shape[0] * L)
        x = x.unflatten(0, (-1, L))
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).reshape(-1, L, 3, H, HD).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4).unbind(0)
        x = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(-1, L, D)
        return self.out(x.flatten(0, 1))


dev, dt = "cuda", torch.bfloat16
m = M().to(dev, dt).eval()
ex = (torch.randn(4 * L, D, device=dev, dtype=dt),
      torch.zeros(4, dtype=torch.long, device=dev))
ep = torch.export.export(m, ex, dynamic_shapes={"x": {0: Dim.AUTO}, "sizes": {0: Dim.AUTO}}, strict=True)
torch._inductor.aoti_compile_and_package(ep, package_path="/tmp/repro.pt2")
aoti = torch._inductor.aoti_load_package("/tmp/repro.pt2")

print(f"torch {torch.__version__}  example bs=4  L={L}  MAXN={MAXN}")
with torch.inference_mode():
    for bs in range(1, MAXN + 1):
        x = torch.randn(bs * L, D, device=dev, dtype=dt)
        s = torch.zeros(bs, dtype=torch.long, device=dev)
        eager_rows = m(x, s).shape[0]
        try:
            aoti_rows = aoti(x, s).shape[0]
            tag = "OK " if aoti_rows == eager_rows else "BAD"
        except Exception:
            aoti_rows, tag = "CRASH", "ERR"
        print(f"  bs={bs}: eager={eager_rows:4d}  aoti={aoti_rows!s:>5}  {tag}")
```

### Observed output (torch 2.9.1+cu128, RTX 3090)

```
torch 2.9.1+cu128  example bs=4  L=1496  MAXN=8
  bs=1: eager=1496  aoti=CRASH  ERR     ← flash_attn: "batch size must be positive" (recovered batch == 0)
  bs=2: eager=2992  aoti= 1496  BAD     ← one image short
  bs=3: eager=4488  aoti= 4488  OK
  bs=4: eager=5984  aoti= 4488  BAD     ← one image short
  bs=5: eager=7480  aoti= 7480  OK
  bs=6: eager=8976  aoti= 8976  OK
  bs=7: eager=10472  aoti=10472  OK
  bs=8: eager=11968  aoti=10472  BAD    ← one image short
```

Runtime warning that points at the root cause:

```
[W Resize.cpp:31] Warning: An output with one or more elements was resized since it had
shape [1496, 3840], which does not match the required output shape [2992, 3840].
```

`[L, 3*D]` = one image's worth of rows = AOTI's compile-time symbolic size for the QKV linear output. The runtime eager fallback resizes it because the true shape needs `bs*L` rows.

### Same bug reproduces on every version tested

| torch | bs=1 | bs=2 | bs=3 | bs=4 | bs=5 | bs=6 | bs=7 | bs=8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.8.0+cu128 | CRASH | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |
| 2.9.1+cu128 | CRASH | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |
| 2.12.0.dev20260408+cu128 | bad (0 rows) | bad | ✓ | bad | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bad |

(2.12 nightly silently returns 0 rows at `bs=1` instead of crashing — same bug, slightly different surface.)

### Pure-Python predictor (no torch needed)

```python
def will_aoti_be_wrong_at(L: int, N: int) -> bool:
    return int((1.0 / L) * (N * L)) != N
```

Verified L-sensitivity (matches AOTI output exactly):

| L | rationale | predicted-bad bs∈[1..16] | observed-bad bs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1024 | `1/L = 2^-10` exactly representable | none | none ✓ |
| 1000 | `(1/L)*L` round-trips to exactly 1.0 | none | none ✓ |
| 1496 | `(1/L)*L = 0.9999999999999999` | {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} | {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} ✓ |
| 1500 | `(1/L)*L` round-trips to exactly 1.0 | none | none ✓ |

(`L=1496` is `34*44`, the Qwen2-VL 640×480 grid — a real shape, not contrived.)


### Root cause

#### Bad C++ in `wrapper.cpp:331` of the bs=1 crash trace

```cpp
int64_t s46 = (1.0/1496.0)*arg4_1_size_0;
```

This recovers the symbolic batch `s46` from `arg4_1.size(0) == 1496*s46` by floating-point reciprocal multiplication and truncation to `int64_t`. `1.0/1496.0` is not exactly representable in IEEE-754, so the product accumulates rounding error and truncates wrong for many inputs:

```
bs=1: q*1496  = 0.9999999999999999       → int64_t cast = 0  → flash_attn crash
bs=2: q*2992  = 1.9999999999999998       → 1                  → 1 image short
bs=3: q*4488  = exactly 3.0              → 3                  → ✓
bs=4: q*5984  = 3.9999999999999996       → 3                  → 1 image short
...
bs=8: q*11968 = 7.999999999999999        → 7                  → 1 image short
```

The wrong `s46` then propagates through every downstream buffer allocation (`{1496L*s46, 3840L}` for the QKV output, etc.).

#### Where this gets emitted

**`torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:331`** (`codegen_symbol`) recovers free symbols from input shapes:

```python
solution = try_solve(sympy.Eq(sym_or_exp, size_symbol), free_symbol)
if solution is not None:
    code.writeline(f"int64_t {free_symbol} = {cexpr(solution[1])};")
```

`try_solve` returns the algebraically correct `Mul(Rational(1, 1496), arg4_1_size_0)`. The expression then goes through `cexpr` (the `CppPrinter`), whose `_print_Rational` at **`torch/utils/_sympy/printers.py:400`** is documented to emit float division:

```python
def _print_Rational(self, expr):
    # Uses float constants to perform FP div
    if expr.q == 1:
        r = f"{expr.p}"
    else:
        r = f"{expr.p}.0/{expr.q}.0"
    return f"static_cast<{INDEX_TYPE}>({r})" if expr.is_integer else r
```

Combined with `ExprPrinter._print_Mul` (just `stringify(args, "*")`), `Mul(Rational(1, 1496), x)` lowers to `(1.0/1496.0)*x`. The outer `int64_t {free_symbol} = …;` then truncates the float to integer, dropping the rounding error into the symbol.

#### Why this was deliberate (and why it's still wrong here)

PR #95698 explicitly switched `_print_Rational` from integer division to FP division to fix `upsample_bilinear2d` / `upsample_nearest` dynamic shapes — those ops need real fractional scale factors `output_h / input_h`. The change was correct for upsample.

PR #146044 reused the same `cexpr` printer for integer dim recovery in AOTI, without realizing that the printer's `Rational` handling assumes float context. Issue #145500 (the motivating bug) used `K=2`, which is exactly representable in IEEE-754 — so the test never tripped the rounding path.


### Proposed fix

**Patch the call site, not the printer.** The type information ("I'm writing into `int64_t`") only exists at `codegen_symbol`; the printer is shared with upsample and other float-context callers.

```python
# torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp_wrapper_cpu.py:codegen_symbol

solution = try_solve(sympy.Eq(sym_or_exp, size_symbol), free_symbol)
if solution is not None:
    expr = solution[1]
    # try_solve returns Mul(Rational(1, K), x); rewrite to CleanDiv so cexpr
    # emits c10::div_floor_integer (exact integer division) instead of
    # (1.0/K.0)*x (FP reciprocal that loses precision when 1/K is not
    # exactly representable in IEEE-754).
    if isinstance(expr, sympy.Mul):
        coeff, rest = expr.as_coeff_Mul()
        if isinstance(coeff, sympy.Rational) and coeff.p == 1 and coeff.q != 1:
            from torch.utils._sympy.functions import CleanDiv
            expr = CleanDiv(rest, coeff.q)
    code.writeline(f"int64_t {free_symbol} = {cexpr(expr)};")
    bound_vars.add(free_symbol)
```

`CleanDiv` is torch's "exact integer division, divisor evenly divides" SymPy op — the constraint `K*s == size` from the export graph guarantees the divisibility. Its existing `CppPrinter._print_FloorDiv` (`printers.py:424`) emits:

```cpp
c10::div_floor_integer(static_cast<int64_t>(arg4_1_size_0), static_cast<int64_t>(1496L))
```

Why patch here and not `try_solve` or `_print_Rational`:

- `try_solve` has 15+ callers across torch (export, ShapeEnv, dynamo, range analysis). Most use the result purely symbolically — they shouldn't be perturbed.
- `_print_Rational` is load-bearing for upsample's fractional scale factors. Touching it regresses PR #95698's original motivation.
- Only `codegen_symbol` (and one or two similar call sites in `tiling_utils.py`) knows the lowering target is `int64_t`. Type-aware lowering belongs at the call site.

Patch was applied locally and verified.

### Verification (post-patch, torch 2.9.1+cu128)

**Patched `wrapper.cpp` line emitted:**

```cpp
int64_t s46 = c10::div_floor_integer(static_cast<int64_t>(arg4_1_size_0), static_cast<int64_t>(1496L));
```

(was: `int64_t s46 = (1.0/1496.0)*arg4_1_size_0;`)

**Minimal repro, L=1496, MAXN=16:**

```
torch 2.9.1+cu128  example bs=4  L=1496  MAXN=16
  bs=1..16: eager == aoti for every batch.  (all OK)
```

**Real-world repro** (Qwen2-VL vision tower at 640×480, 32 attention layers, SDPA + rotary):

```
post-patch: bs=1..8 all OK.
```

**Regression checks:**

- `L=1024`: still all OK (was already correct; patch doesn't disturb it).
- `L=1000`: still all OK (lucky round-trip preserved).
- Upsample dynamic shapes: unchanged (the patch only touches the `Mul(Rational(1,K), x)` pattern coming from `codegen_symbol`'s solver path; upsample's float scale factors flow through different ops and are not affected).

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.9.1+cu128
CUDA used to build PyTorch: 12.8
OS: Linux (x86_64) 6.8.0-84-generic
Python: 3.12.11
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090

```

- 2.8.0+cu128
- 2.12.0.dev20260408+cu128 (nightly)

issues.author: IlyasMoutawwakil
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

custom op with mutations fail compilation under @torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
```
    Found a custom (non-ATen) operator whose output has alias annotations:
    repro::add_into(Tensor(a0!) d, Tensor x) -> ().
    We only support functionalizing operators whose outputs do not have alias
    annotations.
```
```python

import torch


@torch.library.custom_op("repro::add_into", mutates_args=("d",))
def add_into(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    """Compile-aware in-place add: ``d.add_(x)``."""
    d.add_(x)


@add_into.register_fake
def _add_into_fake(d, x):  # noqa: ARG001
    return None


# --- Scenario A: same op, called at top level (no nested_compile_region) ----


def top_level(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    torch.ops.repro.add_into(d, x)
    return d + 1.0


# --- Scenario B: same op, called from inside nested_compile_region ----------


@torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
def nested_inner(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    torch.ops.repro.add_into(d, x)
    return d + 1.0


def with_nested(d: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return nested_inner(d, x)


def main() -> int:
    d = torch.zeros(4, device="cpu")
    x = torch.ones(4, device="cpu")

    # Sanity: eager.
    print("eager top_level   :", top_level(d.clone(), x))
    print("eager with_nested :", with_nested(d.clone(), x))

    failures = 0

    # Scenario A: top-level torch.compile — expected to PASS.
    print()
    print("--- Scenario A: torch.compile(top_level)  [no nested_compile_region] ---")
    compiled_a = torch.compile(top_level, fullgraph=True)
    try:
        out = compiled_a(d.clone(), x)
        print(f"PASS — compiled top-level: {out}")
    except Exception as e:
        failures += 1
        print(f"UNEXPECTED FAIL ({type(e).__name__}): {e}")

    # Scenario B: nested_compile_region inside torch.compile — expected to FAIL on torch 2.12.
    print()
    print("--- Scenario B: torch.compile(with_nested)  [calls nested_compile_region] ---")
    compiled_b = torch.compile(with_nested, fullgraph=True)
    try:
        out = compiled_b(d.clone(), x)
        print(f"PASS — compiled with nested: {out}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"FAIL ({type(e).__name__}): {e}")
        failures += 1

    print()
    if failures == 1:
        print(
            "Summary: top-level works, nested_compile_region path fails — bug confirmed."
        )
        return 0
    print(f"Summary: unexpected outcome (failures={failures}).")
    return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
```

**Claude finished @jansel's task in 9m 13s** —— [View job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/27231514897)

---
### Where this was fixed

@jansel I traced the fix in the code on `main`. Short version: the bug was fixed by **adding `auto_functionalize` support to `invoke_subgraph` (and HOPs generally)**, so a subgraph that mutates its inputs is now routed through `do_auto_functionalize_v2` instead of being passed verbatim to functionalization (which is what produced the `output has alias annotations` error).

#### Root cause
On torch 2.12, `invoke_subgraph`'s functionalization key assumed the subgraph was already functional — *"There is an assumption that subgraph does not mutate inputs and there is no aliasing. It's Dynamo's responsibility to prevent formation of invoke_subgraph ops if input aliasing/mutation is detected."* When a custom op with `mutates_args` lived inside the region, that assumption broke and the mutating op was handed straight to the functionalize pass, which rejects custom ops whose schema carries a write/alias annotation (`Tensor(a0!)`).

#### The fix (on `main`)
`torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py:1020-1099` — the `py_functionalize_impl` now builds a `HopInstance`, and if `can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance)` is true it returns `do_auto_functionalize_v2(...)`:

```python
if can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance):
    # NOTE: [auto_functionalize x invoke_subgraph caching]
    # We call auto_functionalized_v2 to support input mutation of invoke_subgraph.
    # See NOTE [Support input mutation of hops] for the overall design.
    ...
    return do_auto_functionalize_v2(
        ctx.mode, hop_instance,
        (subgraph, "auto_functionalized_" + identifier, *operands), {},
    )
```

The overall design is documented in **`NOTE [Support input mutation of hops]`** at `torch/_higher_order_ops/base_hop.py:133-150`: functionalize the subgraph, inline a `copy_` epilogue, route the HOP through `auto_functionalized_v2`, and let inductor decompose it — the same machinery custom ops already use for input mutation. The matching `can_auto_functionalize(HopInstance)` branch is at `torch/_higher_order_ops/auto_functionalize.py:426-445`.

Regression tests covering exactly your scenario now live in `test/higher_order_ops/test_invoke_subgraph.py`: `test_input_mutation`, `test_input_mutation_mutiple_times`, `test_input_mutation_mutiple_times_fake_tensor_cache_hit`, `test_input_mutation_inference_mode` (lines ~1357-1455).

I couldn't pull the exact PR number from here — this CI checkout is a shallow clone (depth 1), and `gh`/`curl`/`WebFetch`/`git fetch` are all blocked by an ungranted permission prompt in this environment, so I can't query GitHub history. To find it locally, blame the auto_functionalize hook:


(@ydwu4 authored the "input mutation of hops" / auto_functionalize-for-HOPs work and would know the exact PR.)

The `auto_functionalize` machinery wasn't wired into `invoke_subgraph` on 2.12, so you can't get the region to functionalize the mutation itself. Options:

1. **Use `auto_functionalized` semantics at the op boundary.** Custom-op input mutation *does* work at the top level on 2.12 (your Scenario A passes) because top-level functionalization handles `mutates_args` via `auto_functionalized`. The region is the only thing missing that path — so keep the mutating op *outside* `nested_compile_region` and only put pure computation inside it.
2. **Make the region functional.** Return the new tensor from the region instead of mutating in place, and do the in-place write outside:

3. If you must mutate inside, drop `nested_compile_region` for that callsite on 2.12 — top-level `torch.compile` handles the mutating custom op correctly.

issues.title: [Inductor][HOP] FlexAttention should bind derived unbacked tensor input extents from runtime metadata
issues.author: sanketpurandare
issues.body:
## Summary

FlexAttention compilation can fail when graph chunking feeds a regional
FlexAttention call with unbacked symbolic tensor metadata. A common case is a
batch chunk whose extent is a derived expression such as `u0 // 2`, together
with a sequence length that remains symbolic through the FlexAttention lowering
path.

The runtime source of truth for those regional extents is the tensor input
metadata at the compiled boundary. Inductor should bind the exact derived input
size expression from that metadata, and FlexAttention policy decisions should
avoid forcing data-dependent symbolic predicates when the conservative choice is
to keep compiling or fall back to the main FlexAttention kernel.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch
from torch._dynamo.decorators import mark_unbacked
from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import create_block_mask, flex_attention


if not torch.cuda.is_available():
    raise RuntimeError("This repro needs CUDA.")


device = "cuda"
B, H, S, D, MAX_S = 4, 2, 64, 64, 128
stride = (H * MAX_S * D, MAX_S * D, D, 1)


def make_tensor():
    tensor = torch.empty_strided(
        (B, H, S, D), stride, device=device, dtype=torch.float16
    )
    tensor.normal_()
    tensor.requires_grad_(True)
    mark_unbacked(tensor, 0, hint_override=B, shape_id="batch", min=2, max=B)
    mark_unbacked(tensor, 2, hint_override=S, shape_id="seq", min=1, max=MAX_S)
    return tensor


def causal_mask(_b, _h, q_idx, kv_idx):
    return q_idx >= kv_idx


block_mask = create_block_mask(
    causal_mask, B=None, H=None, Q_LEN=S, KV_LEN=S, device=device
)
q, k, v = make_tensor(), make_tensor(), make_tensor()


@torch.compile(dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)
def fn(q, k, v):
    mid = q.shape[0] // 2
    return (
        flex_attention(q[:mid], k[:mid], v[:mid], block_mask=block_mask).sum()
        + flex_attention(q[mid:], k[mid:], v[mid:], block_mask=block_mask).sum()
    )


fn(q, k, v).backward()
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("ok")
```

This is a standalone version of the graph-trainer case: a graph pass chunks a
dynamic batch dimension, preserves symbolic sequence metadata, and compiles
FlexAttention forward/backward inside the chunked region.

## Expected behavior

The compiled FlexAttention forward and backward should complete.

Inductor should bind derived input size expressions such as `u0 // 2` from
runtime tensor input metadata and reuse those bindings when printing symbolic
size variables, symbolic call arguments, and Triton template arguments.

FlexAttention validation and backend-selection predicates should reject only
provably invalid symbolic relations. If a flex-decoding heuristic cannot prove
its symbolic predicates, it should conservatively fall back to the main
FlexAttention kernel.

## Actual behavior

Compilation can fail during Inductor wrapper or template codegen because the raw
parent symbol is expected to have been emitted even though the runtime source is
the input tensor extent for the whole derived expression:

```text
AssertionError: For (u0//2), expected [u0] to have been codegen-ed
```

Nearby FlexAttention validation and backend-selection paths can also force
symbolic predicates on hinted unbacked dimensions and raise data-dependent guard
errors instead of taking the conservative traceable path.

issues.title: [torch.compile] Clarification/regression: Dynamo cache lookup guard eval is much slower in 2.12 vs 2.7 after `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` became always True
issues.author: mihudaner
issues.body: ### 🐛 Describe the bug We are investigating a TorchDynamo cache lookup / guard evaluation performance regression when moving a large inference model from PyTorch 2.7 to a 2.12-based build. This is not currently a correctness issue. The compiled model runs, but the runtime overhead before entering compiled regions is noticeably higher. From `TORCH_LOGS="+guards"` and local profiling, the hot frame guard evaluation / cache lookup cost increased from roughly 1 ms in 2.7 to roughly 3-4 ms in 2.12 for our large decoder-style inference workload. We also noticed that `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` is deprecated in newer PyTorch and effectively always True: ```python inline_inbuilt_nn_modules = Config( default=True, justknob="pytorch/compiler:inline_inbuilt_nn_modules", deprecated=True, deprecation_message="does not do anything, inline_inbuilt_nn_modules is always True", ) ``` The related commit message says: ```text inline_inbuilt_nn_modules has defaulted to True and the False path is legacy. This makes the config a no-op (always True), emits a deprecation warning when users set it to False, and removes all dead False-path code from runtime. ``` However, we could not find a detailed public issue or design note explaining the full motivation and expected behavior changes from this deprecation. Many repeated `nn.Module` layers. 2. Repeated module attributes used in shape computations, such as `top_k`, `spec_len`, `block_size`, `num_heads`, `head_dim`. 3. Module tensor attributes similar to `block_table`, `fa_norm_residual`, `cur_topk_list`. 4. Shared Python objects across layers to trigger alias identity guards. #### Questions 1. What was the full motivation for deprecating `torch._dynamo.config.inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` and making it effectively always True? 2. Is the intended guidance that users should no longer try `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules=False` as a performance workaround? 3. Besides `inline_inbuilt_nn_modules` becoming deprecated/no-op, what other Dynamo guard or cache lookup changes between 2.7 and 2.12 could increase runtime guard eval / cache lookup overhead for large inference graphs? 4. If no config can safely recover 2.7-like lookup overhead in 2.12, what is the recommended mitigation for large repeated-module inference models? Should users refactor code to avoid reading Python/module attributes inside compiled regions, or is there a compiler-side way to reduce repeated guards? cc @ezyang @gchanan @kadeng @msaroufim @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @amjames @jataylo @azahed98

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When wrapping `flex_attention` with `torch.compile(dynamic=True, fullgraph=True)`, we observe NaN in attention output during training with `create_block_mask(_compile=False)`

This suggests the compiled Triton kernel for `flex_attention` introduces a numerical bug ? when combined with: 
- `dynamic=True` (symbolic shapes)
- `fullgraph=True`
- Batch-dependent BlockMask (varying sparsity pattern per iteration)

## Key Code

### Mask (batch-dependent)

`mf` mask allows visual tokens to see future tokens (but not answer tokens):

```python
MOD_VISUAL = 0   # visual token
MOD_TEXT   = 1   # question text token
MOD_ANSWER = 2   # answer text token

def create_mf_mask(sample_id_map, modality_map):
    def mask_mod(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx):
        same_sample = sample_id_map[q_idx] == sample_id_map[kv_idx]
        q_is_visual = modality_map[q_idx] == MOD_VISUAL
        kv_is_visual = modality_map[kv_idx] == MOD_VISUAL
        kv_is_question = modality_map[kv_idx] == MOD_TEXT

        past_causal = q_idx >= kv_idx
        future_v2v = (q_idx < kv_idx) & q_is_visual & kv_is_visual
        future_v2q = (q_idx < kv_idx) & q_is_visual & kv_is_question

        return same_sample & (past_causal | future_v2v | future_v2q)
    return mask_mod
```

issues.title: `torch.remainder` returns incorrect results with float16 tensor and Python scalar on Inductor CPU
issues.author: rookieLiu2018
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with the Inductor CPU backend returns a different result from eager mode for `torch.remainder` when the input is a `float16` tensor and the divisor is a Python float scalar.

### Reproducer

```python
import torch

def f(x):
    return torch.remainder(x, 3.14)

x = torch.tensor(
    [-4.0, -1.5, -0.0, 0.0, 0.1, 1.0, 3.140625, 8.0],
    dtype=torch.float16,
)

eager = f(x)
compiled = torch.compile(f, backend="inductor")(x)

print("eager =", eager)
print("compiled =", compiled)
```

Output:

```text
eager = tensor([2.2812, 1.6406, -0.0000, 0.0000, 0.1000, 1.0000, 0.0000, 1.7188],
       dtype=torch.float16)
compiled = tensor([2.2793e+00, 1.6396e+00, 0.0000e+00, 0.0000e+00, 9.9976e-02, 1.0000e+00,
        6.2466e-04, 1.7197e+00], dtype=torch.float16)
```

### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.10.0+cpu
